L74@P1: work in an arms factory like her father. But the factory turns her down sneeringly. Then
L75@P1: her father gets called up to the Landsturm and the family is poor once again. Lotte wants
L76@P1: to be an actress, but her mother doesn’t agree. So she seeks for a job which will allow her
L77@P1: to express her burning sentiments of chivalry, and chooses Kinderpflege. She receives her
L78@P1: first love letter, from Herbert. She makes friends with Luise, while being obnoxious in her
L79@P1: class. Lotte ceases, painfully, to believe in the warm, loving God of her childhood.
L80@P1: Kap. 5 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 84-101
L81@P1: Lotte is seventeen, and rebellious against the social order. She joins the Freideutsche
L82@P1: Jugend and finds others who share her ideas. Her mother doesn’t want her to come home
L83@P1: late, generating a mixture of lies and quarrels. She meets a girl who puts her in contact
L84@P1: with her brother Helwig, who is at the front in Turkey. Passionate exchange of long letters,
L85@P1: followed by a hilarious though sad description of his arriving on leave to meet her for the
L86@P1: first time, dirty, unkempt and suffering from a bad cold. Long reflection upon the effect of
L87@P1: this cold on her feelings, mingled with self-contempt. In the meantime, Hans is fired from
L88@P1: the bank for stealing. But his boss takes pity on his mother and finds him a job in another
L89@P1: bank.
L90@P1: Kap. 6 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 102-125
L91@P1: Short reminiscences of children; having boots made, going on summer family trip.
L92@P1: Description of semi-abandoned children of Granatendreherin mothers (women working in
L93@P1: arms factories). Transition to Lotte’s studying to become a Kindergarten teacher. The
L94@P1: class is taught by a Kindergarten teacher, Fra¨ulein Rasmussen, whom Lotte likes on sight,
L95@P1-2: 2but then despises because her teaching is so hesitant. Lotte amuses herself by constantly
L96@P2: interrupting to display her superiority. However, when she then becomes a student teacher
L97@P2: under this lady, she discovers that she herself is not good with the children (in spite of all
L98@P2: her good will and belief in the worth of the job, and all her principles), whereas Fr¨aulein
L99@P2: Rasmussen is absolutely wonderful. Description of some frightful little kids. Lotte feels
L100@P2: guilty and stupid, the more so because she starts wondering if this is really the right job for
L101@P2: her. She much prefers taking a day off to run around in nature, singing loudly in storms
L102@P2: and rain, or going on rambles with comrades from the Freideutsche Jugend.
L103@P2: Lotte is annoyed with herself for being strongly physically attracted to a handsome
L104@P2: young man of very average intelligence, who furthermore is a “Bl¨uher-Junge” which means
L105@P2: he reads Bl¨uher and considers women fundamentally inferior. Lotte partly agrees with
L106@P2: this, she finds women’s souls full of “Formlose und Unklare”, contrasted with the “scharfe
L107@P2: m¨annliche Geist”. She even blames all her own defects on this; she has no fondness for the
L108@P2: beauties of femininity, she would like to be strong and bold and keen. Nonetheless, she
L109@P2: resents Ludwig’s assumption of obvious superiority over her since (intellectually) she feels
L110@P2: greatly superior to him, in spite of also feeling “mies und schwer und plump”. She also
L111@P2: makes a friend of a certain kind and intelligent Robert (same name as her father). Her
L112@P2: mother approves highly, but no love is in sight.
L390@P7: about crime, punishment and other issues.
L391@P7: She has interesting conversations with Redy about modern women’s issues such as
L392@P7: ‘Huren’, ‘Abtreibung’, ‘Frauenrauchen’ and so forth. He writes a poem that she loves:
L393@P7: (“Wir sind da und wissen nicht: warum”). We learn a little about Karl Ross. In the
L394@P7: meantime, Lotte’s father has become the head of the boot cleaners in the Hauptbahnhof.
L395@P7: He also rents out bits of soap and clean towels. He hires Lotte to work for him, washing
L396@P7: and ironing 100 towels per day. She also writes for the Pranger, and spends all her evenings
L397@P7-8: 8in the club. Basically she never sleeps.
L398@P8: Redy is still in love with Tamara, and Lotte is eager to meet her but then she is very
L399@P8: disappointed to find that Tamara is gentle and sweet, not her type at all. Redy takes
L400@P8: Lotte home with him, but he is very depressed; he cries. Lotte’s heart is wrenched; she is
L401@P8: really in love with him. She reflects on her idealistic view of mankind and her contempt
L402@P8: for individuals: “Ich liebe den Menschen und glaube an ihn in eben dem Masse, wie ich
L403@P8: die Leute verabscheue und l¨acherlich finde.”
L404@P8: Redy and his friend Bobby go on a two-week walking tour, during which Lotte gets
L405@P8: two postcards asking for money and food, while Tamara gets long passionate letters. Then
L406@P8: Redy returns, but has no place to live. Lotte hides him in a basement room at her parents’
L407@P8: house, and brings in and out all that is necessary, no details spared. Then she has the
L408@P8: humiliation of hearing Redy refer to her as his ‘Waschfrau’. Next, Lotte’s mother tells her
L409@P8: that she asked Redy to take some money and send it to Tante Grete, but he stole it. Redy
L410@P8: admits this, explaining that he needed the money. Lotte is ashamed and wants the money
L411@P8: back: she manages to borrow it from her old friend Edwin Bartels who is still in love with
L412@P8: her.
L413@P8: Kap. 15 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 390-410
L414@P8: An evening in the H.-K.-Diele (the club), with sparkling conversation. But Lotte is
L415@P8: in a black mood because of unrequited love. Finally, her mother calls on Redy to actually
L416@P8: come and console her, as only he can. At this point Redy has left the hiding place, and
L417@P8: now has a small job working in a tiny sordid bookstore lending out adventure books and
L418@P8: a little illegal porn.
L419@P8: Lotte wanders around going to bed with different men to console them for their
L420@P8: ‘Weltschmerz’, and considering herself a heroine for not using any contraceptives, but
L421@P8: giving herself entirely and generously to the man. When the men worry about the possible
L422@P8: consequences, she tells them that it’s her problem, and there are doctors for such things.
L423@P8: This is her version of feminism: not requiring protection.
L424@P8: Suddenly Lotte is distracted from her private life by a new cause: the government puts
L425@P8: forth a proposition to close the government-organized brothels. Lotte is thrilled, and wants
L426@P8: to make use of the Pranger’s influence. But Karl Ross advises her to meet and talk with the
L427@P8: Kontrollm¨adchen first. She does so at length, and finds herself in a terrible dilemma: the
L428@P8: girls are terrified of finding themselves delivered over to the abuses of “private enterprise”
L429@P8: and radically against the closing of the brothels.
L430@P8: In order to defend their rights, Lotte finds herself using the paper to support the rejection of the new law, as the principle of direct human aid vanquishes that of a higher humanity (“Lotte entscheidet sich f¨ur die Butterstullen-Menschlichkeit, gegen das Prinzip.”)
L431@P8: The chapter ends with Lotte meeting a vain young hunchback sculptor who infuriates her
L432@P8: by boasting vainly that he works on converting bourgeois young girls into prostitutes. She
L433@P8: tries to tell him that this is idiotic since prostitutes have as bourgeois a mentality as any,
L434@P8: if not more, but of course that misses the point (which is this gentleman’s own personal
L435@P8: titillation). She comes to realise that her real anger against him is because it means that
L436@P8: her own experience was not a unique destiny but a kind of “scheussliche Modespielerei”.
L463@P9: The next day, Redy and Lotte enter their new room. It is absolutely disgusting, filthy
L464@P9: and smells of vomit. There is a large window but it can’t be opened. Lotte spends the day
L465@P9: scraping, washing and scrubbing, and the room improves slightly. As furniture, she and
L466@P9: Redy have the stolen mattress, a large writing table that is a gift from Karl, three chairs
L467@P9: from Hulda, and an old, broken chocolate machine to use as a cupboard. They decorate
L468@P9: with a rug offered by Karl, and a pretty bedcover that Lotte brought from home. She
L469@P9: sprays perfume around the room, and buys wine and flowers. But the prettier she makes
L470@P9: the room, the heavier and bitterer her heart becomes, until finally she and Redy are alone
L471@P9: in bed together, and he tells her that he loves her and no one else.
L472@P9: IV. Zu Berlin
L473@P9: Kap. 1. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 1-28
L474@P9: A lot about a man that Lotte and Redy meet in a Kneipe; a failed actor ruined by
L475@P9: the war called Freund Jule, who lives by singing and reciting in bars every evening with
L476@P9: a desperate, broken voice. They take him in and insist on keeping him even though he
L477@P9: comes home dead drunk and wails out his life story for hours every single evening, not to
L478@P9: mention vomiting and smelling horrible. Still, he also brings in some money and cooks very
L479@P9: nicely. Lotte is persuaded (to her own surprise) to organize a ridiculous, old-fashioned,
L480@P9: “spiessig” Christmas party with Karl Ross and his wife, who live downstairs, and Lotte’s
L481@P9: friend Maria. But the party is a horrible failure, with Freund Jule falling on his knees and
L482@P9: Maria spitting at him in disgust and dashing out of the house, then Karl Ross getting dead
L483@P9: drunk and attacking his wife and little daughters and smashing everything in the house.
L484@P9: Everybody rushes upstairs for safety and Redy undertakes to soothe Karl: “H¨ochste Zeit,
L485@P9: dass der Papa runterkommt und bisschen Ordning schafft. Mit Besoffenen, Verr¨uckten une
L486@P9: Selbstm¨ordern weiss ich ganz gut umzugehen.”
L487@P9: Kap. 2 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 29-67
L488@P9: Daily life, with little to eat, and even that must be shared with friends. Visits from
L489@P9: various people (prostitutes etc.) asking for help with writing letters. Suddenly one day
L490@P9: – a visit from Betty! Betty is no longer a prostitute, she is now permanently kept by
L491@P9: a kind sailor who only comes every six weeks or so. Very pretty and elegant, but with
L492@P9: a disastrously broken voice. And yet she has moral standards and is shocked by Lott’s
L493@P9: opinions on sex and marriage. Visit by a seventeen-year-old boy who got Redy’s sixteenyear-old sister pregnant. He helps them steal wood for the fire, brings them butter and
L494@P9: cheese. Lotte and Redy discuss unfaithfulness; he wants never to know, she wants to know
L495@P9-10: 10and then “wir gehen voneinander”. “Ich – Ja. Du – Nein.” Betty is homesick and takes to
L496@P10: visiting home, Lotte goes also but mostly to work and earn a little money housecleaning,
L497@P10: and steal briketts. She and Redy write a lot for the Pranger, but earn little. Fortunately,
L498@P10: they supplement it a bit with graphology. Appearance of the Heilige (the Saint), Louis
L499@P10: H¨ausser. Description of his vocal powers and influence, his group of devoted women. He
L500@P10: tries but fails to conquer Lotte. Eye to eye. They catch lice from him. Shame, followed
L501@P10: by interesting necessity of shaving. Freund Jule comes home at a particularly untactful
L502@P10: moment, and ends up thrown out. Lotte and Redy feel guilty but pleased. Horrible evening
L503@P10: in a bar with gloomy drunk Betty. When they return, they hear the return of old Hulda’s
L504@P10: ancient boyfriend, newly released from prison. They hear talking and singing, followed by
L505@P10: horrible screams. They rush in and rescue Hulda whose face is smashed.
L506@P10: Kap. 3 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 68-93
L507@P10: Lotte is pregnant. She wonders if it is not from a one-time event with the seventeenyear-old. She wishes that Redy would get a regular job, to ensure her a little rest, and a
L508@P10: calm and happy pregnancy. But he doesn’t even think of it. She eventually realizes that
L509@P10: their love is beyond such things. She doesn’t want to bring up a child in their disgusting
L510@P10: room at old Hulda’s, but Redy thinks that what matters isn’t where you bring up the
L511@P10: child, but how. Karl Ross kidnaps a child who is about to be separated from its mother
L512@P10: and taken to the orphanage. Reflections on children; Lotte feels that they should all be
L513@P10: removed from their parents and brought up in lovely homes with eight or ten children to
L514@P10: two or three understanding adults. A strange lady comes, having left her family and sold
L515@P10: her house, to give her entire fortune to the Heilige. She wants him to make her pregnant.
L516@P10: He takes all the money, throws her out and spends it in a brothel. Redy spends a week
L517@P10: in Berlin at a sexology conference (photos of him with Magnus Hirschfeld). They write
L518@P10: so much for the Pranger that they almost run out of ideas. But they always refuse to
L519@P10: publish anything written by the Heilige, even though he offers to pay generously. Lotte’s
L520@P10: father decides to rent a decent room for them, in spite of his loathing of Redy. But the new
L521@P10: landlady insists that they get married (accusing them of “Kuppelei”). So they do, although
L522@P10: both their fathers are strongly against it. Hans comes out of prison and after working on
L523@P10: a farm, and returns home to join his father in the successful Bahnhof-Stiefelputzerei.
L524@P10: Kap. 4 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 94-112
L525@P10: Unbelievably, Karl Ross got drunk and sold the Pranger. Redy and Lotte have to
L526@P10: stop working for it, and slowly begin to starve. The newspaper, taken over by a couple
L527@P10: of idiots, fails after a few months. The couple sells their things, and visits friends to eat
L528@P10: or even just for tea and sugar. They eat at most once a day. Out of idealism, Lotte
L644@P12: rooms. Then, rested, with ironed clothes, they go to Mosse. But when they get there,
L645@P12: Redy refusees to go in, so Lotte goes alone, lips pressed together. It’s a success; he’ll take
L646@P12: anything she writes, and Redy can work as a theater critic (she mentions his panning the
L647@P12-13: 13actor Alexander Moissi). However, Lotte finds that she can’t work enough, because she
L648@P13: has to take care of Frigga all day, and moreover, to her surprise, she is turning into a
L649@P13: perfectly typical housewife. She remembers saying that she would never do that; that if
L650@P13: she worked professionally, then she and her husband would always share the housework,
L651@P13: that any man could mend socks as well as she could. But suddenly, she notices that she’s
L652@P13: cooking and mending socks. She talks it over with Redy very reasonably, but he answers,
L653@P13: also very reasonably, that he would rather have holes in his socks than mend them himself. She is annoyed that he always seems busy and yet doesn’t really do much. Some of
L654@P13: Lotte’s best stories are rejected because they are too artistic; then they are accepted by
L655@P13: the Welt am Abend, but it turns out to be a communist paper, and Lotte quarrels with
L656@P13: the redaction. She decides to take Frigga back to her parents for a while so as to be able
L657@P13: to work harder, and to buy Redy a proper suit, as she thinks maybe his tired, wrinkled
L658@P13: suit may be psychologically responsible for his tired, wrinkled soul. This earned, she offers
L659@P13: herself her first ever self-earned custom-tailored suit. She wears it to Hamburg to bring
L660@P13: the child to her parents. When there, she meets with all her old friends, particularly Bert
L661@P13: Reinicke. That night she’s in bed with him. The next day is her parent’s silver wedding,
L662@P13: and that is when Lotte realizes that her mother is not happy, has never been happy...
L663@P13: Kap. 12 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 297-318
L664@P13: Lotte can’t keep a secret from Redy; Bert’s love letters and his eager visit to Berlin
L665@P13: are soon revealed. Redy proposes a one-night triangle, Lotte accepts, Bert finds himself
L666@P13: caught up in it. Details of the triangular event; Bert seems anguished (by prejudice, thinks
L667@P13: Lotte). He leaves. She decides to follow him back to Hamburg. Redy says he’s coming
L668@P13: too. It takes them three weeks to get the money together, then they go, only for Lotte to
L669@P13: receive a letter from Bert saying that he has met another girl. Redy is naturally pleased.
L670@P13: They spend their evenings in the H.-K.-Diele. Little Frigga doesn’t recognize her mother
L671@P13: any more after her long stay with her grandparents, and Lotte determines to rent a little
L672@P13: house in Berlin and bring her home.
L673@P13: Kap. 13 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 319-339
L674@P13: Lotte and Redy have rented a little house with a garden, in readiness for Frigga’s
L675@P13: return to her parents. Redy brings home a charming new friend, Richard. A few days
L676@P13: later, Redy having gone upstairs to his room, Lotte and Richard fall into each others arms
L677@P13: passionately. But Redy comes back downstairs again. He walks out, and Lotte continues
L678@P13: a very casual affair with Richard, until a couple of weeks later. This is the day when
L679@P13: Lotte’s mother arrives, bringing Frigga. Lotte has to tell her that Redy is gone, and why.
L680@P13: Her mother is amazed, remembering how her daughter and wanted to have her Redy at
L681@P13: any price, but not absolutely displeased. She spends a while in the peaceful garden, and
L682@P13: prepares a nice chicken for dinner. But Redy reappears and demands that Lotte make her
L683@P13: mother leave for Hamburg at once. Tears. Lotte does it, against her will, then feels guilty
L684@P13: and is furious with Redy.
L685@P13: Kap. 14 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 340-376
L686@P13: Redy is by this time totally incapable of working. He spends all day at his desk or in
L687@P13: his atelier, frequently rearranging his papers, and that’s it. Nor will he ever take care of
L688@P13: the baby. Lotte takes care of her, walks two hours to the newspaper offices and then back,
L689@P13: and writes all night, hardly sleeping. In the morning when she wakes up, she finds the baby
L690@P13: in its bed, happy but filthy, because she simply can’t sleep even less than she already does.
L691@P13: Even so, she alone can’t make enough money to pay the rent on the house. By chance,
L692@P13: she runs into Freund Jule and they take him in, but eventually they are obliged to leave
L693@P13: the house, and move to a tent in a camping site on a lake. Lotte meets Dr. Fischer on
L694@P13: the street and he tells her that he was looking everywhere for her; he put together a whole
L695@P13: special issue on “die grosse Strasse”. But now it’s too late; it has to be ready in three days.
L696@P13: For three days and nights, she and Redy write like mad; one thousand lines. But they
L697@P13-14: 14know that what they’re writing isn’t very good, and it comes back rejected. Redy enjoys
L698@P14: the camping site, which makes good use of his talents for pottering around. It becomes
L699@P14: harder than ever for Lotte to write anything, except in the middle of the night. Finally,
L700@P14: at the newspaper office, Lotte is sent to meet Christine Gebhard, a woman who devotes
L701@P14: her life to the work of a dead poet and playwright called Brennmacher. A saintly figure,
L702@P14: Christine lives in a large, beautiful apartment of glass cubes, and she invites Lotte to come
L703@P14: and live in half of it, together with Redy and Frigga. It’s like a miracle. Alas, even in the
L704@P14: handsome apartment, with a desk of his own, Redy does nothing; less, even, than before.
L705@P14: He lies on the bed with his hands behind his head and refuses to feed the baby even when
L706@P14: Lotte has to go to the newspaper. Furious, she calls him a word starting with A. Then she
L707@P14: can’t believe that her marriage, and her endless all-resistant love for Redy has now come
L708@P14: to this.
L709@P14: V. Die Ubergabe ¨
L710@P14: Kap. 1. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 1-33
L711@P14: This volume begins with Redy all alone in Berlin, as Lotte has departed furiously
L712@P14: back to Hamburg with the baby, and Christine Gebhard naturally put him out. In the
L713@P14: Antikriegsmuseum, he meets Hannes, who lets him sleep in his small room. Through
L714@P14: Hannes he meets the circle of anarchists: Gerd∗, Rolland, Margot, Icke, Otto and others.
L715@P14: Redy hangs out with them, and writes long letters to Lotte in the hopes of impressing her
L716@P14: with his anarchist tendencies, so that she will return to him. He visits a dying youth in
L717@P14: the hospital with Margot.
L718@P14: Kap. 2 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 34-57
L719@P14: In particular he tries to impress her by frequently mentioning the soon-to-arrive Russian anarchist Sascha, who looms larger than life over the anarchist milieu. Sascha arrives
L720@P14: and comes to sleep in Hannes’ room. Redy shows him pictures of Lotte, and tells him
L721@P14: about his miseries. Sascha looks at the pictures and says “I will steal your wife from you”.
L722@P14: He then takes his revolver and goes to do the business he came for, which involves revenge
L723@P14: against a miserable Russian anarchist called Andrej. The revenge fails because he feels
L724@P14: sorry for Andrej.
L725@P14: Kap. 3 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 58-76
L726@P14: Lotte returns, and Redy picks her up at the station and takes her back to Hannes’
L727@P14: place. She is horrified at the miserable situation, but they have no choice, so she installs
L728@P14: herself there, adopting the armchair as her personal throne, and allows all the anarchists
L729@P14: to come and pay court. Sascha soon comes, and they fall in love.
L730@P14: Kap. 4 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 77-101
L731@P14: In this chapter, we visit Margot in her own miserable room, and learn about Sascha’s
